angle: River-network structure: graph neural networks vs cheap mass-balance topology features
verdict:
EVIDENCE-QUALITY WARNING, READ FIRST: this angle contains ZERO VERIFIED CLAIMS. Its original search agent died and the angle was re-researched after the adversarial verification stage had already been cut for budget. Every finding below is TIER-3 UNVERIFIED and every finding carries confidence 'unverified'. The documented failure mode of this corpus is confident overreach from thin evidence -- a right conclusion attached to a wrong warrant, a misattributed effect size, or a misdescribed split protocol -- so NO numeric figure below (RMSE values, percentage gains, node counts, R2 values) may be used as the warrant for a project decision until it is checked against the primary source. Direction-of-effect and 'this dataset/route exists' are the load-bearing content here; the numbers are leads, not evidence.

SUBSTANTIVE VERDICT: PURSUE THE CHEAP HALF, DROP THE EXPENSIVE HALF. Do NOT build a graph neural network over the 85-site network. Three independent lines of unverified-but-mutually-consistent evidence point the same way: (a) every published river-network GNN success we could locate was demonstrated on a graph that was 43-100% GAUGED (Delaware 42 segments with 32 temperature-monitored; HydroNets 39- and 13-node fully gauged trees), which is the opposite of an arbitrary Iowa map pin; (b) the reported gains are small and regime-dependent -- they appear under extreme label sparsity and shrink toward noise at full data, and the Iowa dataset (160k near-daily site-days) is the full-data regime; (c) at the specific case that dominates the deployment target -- a headwater pin with no monitored upstream neighbor -- the graph architecture alone reportedly performed WORSE than a plain non-graph model. Add to that the architectural disqualifier: HydroNets keeps per-node parameters and transductive GNNs require the test node to exist in the training graph, so neither can be instantiated at a novel pin at all.

WHAT IS WORTH DOING: use topology as STATIC FEATURES, not as an architecture. Strahler stream order, total and incremental upstream drainage area, arbolate sum, network position (distance to nearest downstream confluence, fraction of basin area above the outlet confluence), reach slope, and drainage density are all computable at an arbitrary ungauged pin from NHDPlus V2 via the NLDI navigation the product already performs, cost roughly one join, and are pure BETWEEN-SITE static information -- exactly the term where the project's headroom lives (between_r2 0.21). Two adjacent moves are higher-value still and are network-topology-adjacent rather than GNN-shaped: (1) adopt PRE-ACCUMULATED, ALREADY-ROUTED catchment attributes (EPA StreamCat 'Ws' metrics, Wieczorek/USGS accumulated NHDPlus attributes), which fix the known Iowa inner-join under-count for multi-state basins for free because the accumulation is done nationally upstream of you; (2) use SPARROW's published per-reach mean-annual nitrogen yield as a single static between-site level prior feature at the outlet COMID -- this is the mass-balance half of the question delivered as a number you can join, requiring no upstream observation.

WHAT MUST BE STATED PLAINLY: the mass-balance half of this angle is largely UNANSWERED. The one survey we hit contained no SPARROW or incremental-area load-estimation literature at all, and the primary SPARROW documentation (USGS TM 6-B3) returned HTTP 403 on every fetch, so all SPARROW claims here are second-hand from agency web pages. Also decisive and unverified-but-categorical: SPARROW's accurate 'conditioned' predictions substitute OBSERVED upstream station loads, which an arbitrary pin can never have; only the weaker 'unconditioned' mode is available to this product, and the one accuracy figure we found for unconditioned ungauged reaches (55-76% relative RMSE on a LONG-TERM MEAN ANNUAL flux) is both a weak bar and not remotely comparable to a daily LOFO number. Finally, the single most decision-relevant finding in the whole corpus is not about topology at all: a CONUS prediction-in-unmonitored-basins study reportedly found that ONE POOLED model beat regionally-grouped models in 14 of 17 regions, that grouped models collapsed precisely where groups were SMALL, and that adding STATIC CATCHMENT ATTRIBUTES produced the single largest error reduction -- with no graph architecture involved. At n=19 independent basin families, that is the shape of the remedy: pool more sites (including out-of-state Upper Mississippi nitrate networks), add static attributes, do not add architecture.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED (tier 3; no adversarial verification was performed on this claim). The most decision-relevant published result located for this angle involves no graph architecture at all: a CONUS stream-temperature prediction-in-unmonitored-basins study reportedly trained on 782 data-rich sites and evaluated on 580 disjoint held-out 'unmonitored' sites, and found that a SINGLE POOLED model beat regionally-grouped and cluster-grouped models in 14 of 17 hydrologic regions, with the grouped models collapsing specifically where groups were SMALL. Adding STATIC CATCHMENT ATTRIBUTES was reportedly the largest single error reduction, larger than adding river discharge. If this holds, it says the Iowa remedy at n=19 families is (a) pool more sites rather than partition, and (b) invest in static between-site attributes -- not in network architecture. Treat all quoted magnitudes as unverified leads.
findings.effectSize: UNVERIFIED figures: pooled model median per-site RMSE reportedly 1.43 degC vs up to 9.09 degC for a small-group regional model (Souris-Red-Rainy) and up to 8.70 degC for a cluster model; adding GAGES-II static attributes reportedly 1.78 -> 1.47 degC (-17%), adding discharge 1.78 -> 1.57 degC (-12%), both combined 1.43 degC. Deep-groundwater-influenced sites 2.00 degC vs 1.26 degC for atmospherically-driven sites.
findings.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout (782 data-rich training sites; 580 disjoint data-poor sites held out and treated as unmonitored) -- as described in an unverified extraction; protocol description itself is unverified
findings.nBasins: 1,362 sites (782 train / 580 held-out unmonitored); an extended experiment reportedly used 2,999 sites with 1,346 training
findings.feasibilityAtN19: The FINDING is feasible and directly applicable at n=19 -- it is an argument AGAINST partitioning and FOR pooling plus static attributes, both of which cost nothing. But note the evidence base is 1,362 sites, roughly 70x our effective independent units, so the demonstration itself could not be reproduced here. The actionable read is directional, not quantitative: at 19 families we are inside the 'very small groups' failure regime this paper reportedly documents, which argues for pooling with out-of-state sites (Illinois, Minnesota, Missouri, Upper Mississippi nitrate networks) before any modelling change.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: Yes for the static-attribute half -- catchment attributes are computable at an arbitrary pin. Partly no for the discharge half: the reported -12% from adding river discharge requires a discharge estimate at the target, which the Iowa product does not have (only 22 of 85 sites have any discharge, zero IWQIS sites). Any attempt to replicate the discharge gain would need modelled/regionalised flow, not observed.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED (tier 3). Multiple extractions converge on a single structural message: the gaged-to-ungaged transfer penalty dominates the architecture choice by more than an order of magnitude. In a 70-segment upper Delaware stream-temperature forecasting study under spatial cross-validation, RMSE at spatially held-out sites was roughly DOUBLE that at gauged sites, while the spread across all four architectures tested -- LSTM, LSTM with data assimilation, RGCN, RGCN with data assimilation -- was reportedly a small fraction of that gap. I.e. whether river-network graph structure was used AT ALL mattered far less than whether the site was monitored. This is the strongest single argument in the corpus against 'a graph architecture is what unlocks unmonitored-node prediction', and it directly parallels the Iowa within_r2 0.42 vs between_r2 0.21 diagnosis. Numbers unverified.
findings.effectSize: UNVERIFIED: 1-day-lead RMSE reportedly 1.45-1.52 degC gauged vs 3.18-3.27 degC ungauged (~2.2x); 7-day lead 1.89-1.99 vs 3.26-3.39 degC. Architecture spread across all four models at ungauged sites reportedly only ~0.09 degC, versus a ~1.7 degC gauged/ungauged gap -- roughly 20x.
findings.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout (5-fold spatial CV; per fold 6 test segments withheld -- 2 mainstem, 2 headwater, 2 reservoir-impacted -- plus 3-4 validation segments)
findings.nBasins: 70 river segments within a single basin (upper Delaware)
findings.feasibilityAtN19: The demonstration used 70 segments in one contiguous, densely monitored basin -- more nodes than our 19 families but the same order as our 85 sites. Reproducing the comparison here is feasible in principle; but the finding argues you should not bother, because the term it identifies as dominant (spatial transfer) is not addressed by the architecture change under test.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: The finding is ABOUT the ungauged pin case and is the honest baseline expectation for it: expect substantial degradation at a novel pin regardless of architecture. The RGCN-with-data-assimilation variant does NOT work at an ungauged pin (see the data-assimilation finding below).

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED (tier 3). NEGATIVE RESULT, the most deployment-relevant one in this angle: in the Delaware River Basin physics-guided recurrent graph network work, the graph architecture ALONE (no process-model pre-training) was reportedly WORSE than a plain per-segment RNN at a HELD-OUT HEADWATER segment for streamflow, and worse again under cross-segment distribution shift (trained on high-flow segments, tested on low-flow segments). The authors' stated reason is mechanical and transfers directly: graph convolution has nothing to aggregate at a node with no upstream neighbours, and 'information propagated from neighbors may not always be helpful if neighboring segments have very different streamflow patterns.' This is precisely the arbitrary-Iowa-map-pin case -- most randomly dropped pins land on small headwater catchments with zero monitored upstream neighbours. Magnitudes unverified; the headwater case is reportedly n=1 segment, so the direction is a strong lead but the size is not evidence.
findings.effectSize: UNVERIFIED: held-out headwater streamflow RMSE reportedly RGrN 1.271 vs RNN 0.879 cms (graph ~45% worse); recovered only by adding process pre-training plus a contrastive loss (0.785). Low-flow spatial-transfer experiment reportedly RGrN 4.073 vs RNN 3.012 (graph ~35% worse), recovering to 2.099 only with pre-training + contrastive loss. At other held-out flow nodes RGrN reportedly barely helped or hurt (Seg C 2.151 -> 2.139; Seg E 11.828 -> 12.078).
findings.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout (target segment's training observations deleted, scored on that segment only) combined with a temporal split (train Oct 1980-Sep 2004, test Oct 2004-Sep 2016); plus a separate high-flow-train / low-flow-test spatial-transfer experiment
findings.nBasins: 42 river segments in one basin; the headwater failure case is a single segment (n=1)
findings.feasibilityAtN19: Highly relevant at n=19 and cheap to heed: it says do not spend the 19 families' worth of statistical budget on a message-passing layer whose benefit is conditional on having informative gauged neighbours. Our topology coverage is 28 upstream_uid / 40 downstream_uid links across 85 sites -- a sparse, mostly disconnected graph, which is the low-connectivity regime where this negative result bites hardest.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: NO -- this is a documented FAILURE at the ungauged-pin analogue. A graph term buys nothing, and may cost, at a node with no gauged upstream neighbour.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED (tier 3). The one genuine held-out-NODE experiment located in the river-network GNN literature is small and heavily qualified. In the 42-segment Delaware network, observations were deleted one segment at a time for five segments (A-E) and the model scored only on that segment. For stream TEMPERATURE the graph-plus-physics model reportedly beat the segment-agnostic RNN at the held-out node in 5 of 5 cases; but (a) it is n=5 nodes with no confidence intervals across nodes, (b) the authors reportedly state there was 'only one segment in the data set for which we have no training data but sufficient testing data' -- so the genuinely-never-observed evidence base is a SINGLE node and the 5-segment result is a SIMULATION of ungauged conditions at sites that are in fact gauged, and (c) even the best model degraded substantially once a segment's own history was removed. The direction (topology partially substitutes for a site's own history, but only partially) is the useful signal; the effect sizes are unverified and the sample is tiny.
findings.effectSize: UNVERIFIED held-out-node temperature RMSE, best graph+physics model vs plain RNN: Seg A 2.501 vs 3.328 (-25%), Seg B 1.205 vs 1.384 (-13%), Seg C 1.589 vs 1.804 (-12%), Seg D 1.297 vs 1.805 (-28%), Seg E 1.345 vs 1.646 (-18%). Penalty for removing a segment's own observations, best model: +20% to +61% RMSE (e.g. Seg C 0.989 -> 1.589); plain RNN penalty reportedly +24% to +89%. Note one extraction reports RGrN at Seg D as 0.902 -> 1.597 while another omits it; the corpus is not internally consistent at the per-segment level.
findings.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout (leave-one-segment-out, own observations deleted from training) nested inside a temporal split
findings.nBasins: 5 segments held out one at a time out of 42; reportedly only 1 truly never-observed segment exists in the dataset
findings.feasibilityAtN19: The demonstration graph (42 segments) is the SAME order of magnitude as our 85 sites / 19 families, so this is genuine evidence that river-network methods do not intrinsically require CAMELS-scale samples. BUT the monitored fraction is the binding constraint, not the node count: 32 of 42 segments (76%) had temperature observations. Our deployment scenario has monitored fraction ~0 in the neighbourhood of a novel pin.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: Only in the weak, simulated sense used here -- one node blanked out inside an otherwise 76%-monitored graph. It does NOT establish performance at a pin embedded in an unmonitored neighbourhood, which is the actual product.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED (tier 3). The published graph gain appears to be a LABEL-SPARSITY phenomenon that collapses in the data-dense regime the Iowa project is actually in. In the Delaware work the advertised headline improvements over a plain RNN were reportedly obtained by randomly subsampling training labels down to 0.1% of site-days; as the label fraction rises toward 100% the graph advantage reportedly shrinks toward noise, and the architecture-only graph variant ends up essentially tied with the physics-pre-trained one at full data. FALSIFIABLE IMPLICATION: the Iowa dataset is 160,074 near-daily site-days over ~85 sites -- the 100%-label regime -- so the published headline gain is the wrong number to extrapolate from. All magnitudes unverified.
findings.effectSize: UNVERIFIED temperature RMSE (degC), graph+physics vs plain RNN: at 0.1% labels 2.464 vs 3.234 (-24%); at 2% labels 1.636 vs 1.908 (-14%); at 100% labels 1.402 vs 1.546 (-9.3%), with the architecture-only graph variant at 1.408 -- i.e. graph convolution reportedly bought ~0.006 degC over its own non-pre-trained variant at full data. Streamflow at 100% labels: RNN 4.406, RGrN 4.139, graph+physics 4.076-4.106 (a wash).
findings.splitProtocol: temporal-holdout (all ML models global, trained on the first 24 years and tested on the next 12 at the SAME segments; label fraction subsampled at random within the training window). NOT comparable to our LOFO 0.820 -- this must never be cited as ungauged-basin evidence.
findings.feasibilityAtN19: Argues against feasibility of a payoff here for a different reason than sample size: even where the method works, the regime that makes it work (severe label scarcity in time) does not describe this project. Our scarcity is in independent SPATIAL units, which is not what the sparsity ablation varied.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: Not applicable -- these are gauged-node, held-out-time-period numbers. Their existence in the abstract of the source is a trap: the headline percentage is a temporal-holdout, sparse-label figure and reads as if it were a transfer result.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED (tier 3). The Delaware graph model's ungauged-node gain is reportedly INSEPARABLE from a calibrated process-based simulator, which the Iowa project does not have an equivalent of. The best variants require PRMS-SNTemp (Precipitation-Runoff Modeling System coupled to a Stream Network Temperature Model, ~84 parameters) to be run on every date at every segment 1980-2016 to supply BOTH dense pre-training targets AND three of the ten input features (shade fraction, solar radiation, potential evapotranspiration). Remove the pre-training and the architecture-only variant is what produces the headwater and distribution-shift failures above. There is no free, publicly runnable, calibrated daily-stream-NITRATE simulator for Iowa that could supply the analogous dense pseudo-label field, so the transferable ingredient of this paper is unavailable to us. The residual deployable ingredient is topology as STATIC FEATURES.
findings.effectSize: UNVERIFIED: pre-training contribution at 0.1% labels, temperature RMSE reportedly RGrN 2.849 -> +pretrain 2.556 (-10.3%) -> +pretrain+contrastive 2.464 (-13.5% vs RGrN); streamflow RGrN 6.299 -> 5.824 (-7.5%).
findings.splitProtocol: mixed -- pre-training ablations reported under the temporal holdout; the recovery-from-failure results under the spatial holdout
findings.feasibilityAtN19: Infeasible as published. Building or calibrating an Iowa daily nitrate process model is far outside the acquisition constraint (no paid data, no field campaigns) and would itself need calibration data we do not have. A partial, cheap substitute worth testing: use SPARROW's published mean-annual per-reach nitrogen yield as a static prior feature rather than as a pre-training target -- see datasets.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: The pre-training route: no, not without a simulator. The static-feature substitute: yes -- SPARROW reach yields and NHDPlus topology attributes are both joinable at an arbitrary pin with no local observation.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED (tier 3). HydroNets -- the other flagship river-network architecture -- is architecturally DISQUALIFIED for an arbitrary map pin, on three independent grounds, and provides zero published evidence for unmonitored-node prediction. (1) Each node reportedly holds three sub-models of which two are BASIN-SPECIFIC with per-node parameters (a combiner and a prediction head); only a middle 'shared hydrologic model' has shared weights, so a novel pin has no trained head to instantiate. (2) The model reportedly takes the target gauge's OWN past readings as an input feature, and its headline metric is defined against a persistence baseline that is undefined without local observations. (3) Evaluation was reportedly a TEMPORAL holdout only -- four monsoon seasons train, one test, every evaluated basin present during training -- with no leave-node-out or ungauged experiment anywhere in the paper. Reported gains are therefore gains at GAUGED nodes over held-out time, not transfer.
findings.effectSize: N/A -- architectural and protocol claims. Corroborating unverified detail: the same paper reportedly states its implementation 'does not include static features' and instantiates all sub-models as LINEAR, and lists static basin features as future work -- so it contains no evidence at all about the between-site absolute-level problem that is this project's actual deficit.
findings.splitProtocol: temporal-holdout (five monsoon periods Jun-Oct 2014-2018; first four years train, fifth test)
findings.nBasins: 52 gauged basins (39 Brahmaputra + 13 Ganga), all seen in training
findings.feasibilityAtN19: Not applicable -- the method cannot be evaluated for our question because it cannot represent an unseen node at all. Independent corroboration from a second source in this corpus: the Delaware authors reportedly characterise HydroNets as focusing 'on predicting basins that are well monitored' and 'limited in generalizing to different scenarios or learning with less data.'
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: NO, categorically. Both the inputs (own past gauge readings) and the parameterisation (per-node weights) presuppose a gauged target. Do not propose HydroNets for this product.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED (tier 3). Where HydroNets DOES apply -- a fully gauged tree, temporal holdout -- its gain over a structure-free flat baseline is reportedly SMALL at typical sites and concentrated in a handful of sites where the baseline had already catastrophically failed, and it made predictions WORSE at 12 of 52 basins (23%). The pattern matters more than the numbers: river-structure priors here mainly rescue broken sites rather than lift working ones, and the largest single degradation was reportedly larger in magnitude than the median improvement. If that pattern holds, adding network structure to an already-functioning Iowa model (LOFO AUC 0.820) is exactly the regime where the published gain is smallest.
findings.effectSize: UNVERIFIED: median improvement reportedly ~+0.01 to +0.03 R2-persist; 39/52 basins improved, 12/52 worse, 1 tie. Mean improvement +0.049 (Brahmaputra) falling to +0.022 excluding three outliers; +0.070 (Ganga) falling to +0.021 excluding two. Headline gains came from sites where the baseline had NEGATIVE skill (e.g. -0.440 -> 0.223). Worst regression -0.056.
findings.splitProtocol: temporal-holdout
findings.feasibilityAtN19: The node counts (39 and 13) are BELOW our 85 sites, which is a genuine counterexample to 'network-structure methods need 300+ basins' -- but the sample-complexity reduction claimed is in TEMPORAL samples per gauged node, not in the number of independent SPATIAL units, and every node in those trees is gauged. Our binding constraint (19 independent spatial units, unmonitored deployment neighbourhood) is untouched by this evidence.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: No. Every result is at a gauged node.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED (tier 3). A survey of ML for prediction in unmonitored water-resources settings reportedly identifies only THREE studies applying GNNs to unmonitored-site prediction (Sun et al. 2021a; Jia et al. 2021b; Bao et al. 2021), NONE of which is a water-quality or nutrient application -- two are stream temperature, one streamflow -- and reports NO quantitative held-out-node error metrics for any of them. If accurate, this is a coverage statement of the strongest kind for this angle: there is no published GNN result demonstrating a quantified gain for NITRATE or nutrient prediction at a held-out node. The survey also reportedly warns that models in its scope are validated on 'pseudo-unmonitored sites' where data is withheld to MIMIC real unmonitored conditions -- i.e. the whole literature's ungauged evidence is simulated, matching the single-truly-ungauged-node caveat in the Delaware work.
findings.effectSize: Absence-of-evidence claim; no metrics reported in the survey for any of the three GNN studies.
findings.splitProtocol: not-applicable (survey-level)
findings.nBasins: 3 GNN studies; reportedly 530 basins (Sun et al.), 42 river segments (Bao et al., Delaware), unstated (Jia et al. 2021b). Of 40 tabulated studies overall, the water-quality entries are reportedly Kalin et al. 2010 (8 river WQ variables), Noori et al. 2020 (3 nutrient loads, MONTHLY, SWAT output into an ANN), and Zhi et al. 2021 (daily dissolved oxygen, 236 CAMELS watersheds); 9 of 40 use CAMELS (671 catchments), 27 of 40 are US-based.
findings.feasibilityAtN19: Not a method -- a scoping result. Its practical force is that adopting a river-network GNN for daily nitrate at ungauged Iowa pins would be an unprecedented application, not a transfer of a demonstrated technique, and would have to be justified from scratch at n=19.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: N/A. The finding is that nothing in this literature has been SHOWN to work at a genuinely ungauged pin for a nutrient target.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED (tier 3). Two survey-level results jointly kill the cheap version of 'just add a GNN'. (a) At n=530 CAMELS basins, reportedly TWO of THREE GNN architectures tested (ChebNet-LSTM, GCN-LSTM) performed WORSE in median cross-basin performance than a standard LSTM; only GraphWaveNet beat it, and the graph approach is elsewhere characterised as only 'slightly' outperforming simple feature concatenation. (b) The graph in that study was reportedly NOT river-network topology but a pairwise-Euclidean-distance / site-characteristic similarity matrix, and the survey makes the explicit design criticism that such a graph 'introduces no new information (e.g., physical connectivity) beyond what' is already in the site characteristics. DIRECT IMPLICATION: a similarity graph over our 85 sites is redundant with the static site features XGBoost already ingests (lat, lon, log_basin_area, distances). Only a TRUE upstream-downstream connectivity graph could add information -- and ours covers just 28 upstream_uid / 40 downstream_uid links.
findings.effectSize: UNVERIFIED: 2 of 3 GNN architectures below standard LSTM in median cross-basin performance at n=530; the single winner described only as 'slightly' better than a concatenated-input baseline. No numeric NSE/RMSE reported in the survey.
findings.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout as characterised in the survey (both transductive and inductive cases discussed); the survey does not give enough detail to confirm the protocol independently
findings.feasibilityAtN19: The evidence base is 530 basins, ~28x our effective independent units. If two of three graph architectures lose to a plain LSTM with 530 basins of training signal, the prior that they would win at 19 families is very poor. This is a case where the n=19 flag reinforces rather than complicates the conclusion.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: The similarity-graph variant would technically be constructible at a new pin (its edges are distance/characteristic based, computable anywhere) -- but by the survey's own argument it would add nothing beyond features already present. The connectivity-graph variant is the only informative one and is unavailable at an unmonitored pin's neighbourhood.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED (tier 3). DEPLOYMENT BLOCKER, architectural: TRANSDUCTIVE GNNs reportedly require that 'both training and testing entities must be present in the graph' at training time, and introducing new test nodes changes how information diffuses without re-training; only INDUCTIVE GNNs can predict on new nodes without retraining. Compounding this, the only architecture reported to beat a plain LSTM at n=530 (GraphWaveNet) is also the only inductive-capable one, while the two transductive variants are the ones that LOST. For an arbitrary Iowa map pin -- a node absent from the training graph by definition -- every transductive GNN in this literature is disqualified before any accuracy question is asked. If a graph model is ever tried here, inductive-only is a hard requirement, not a preference.
findings.effectSize: Architectural constraint. UNVERIFIED supporting pattern: transductive variants below LSTM median, inductive-capable variant above, at n=530.
findings.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout as characterised in the survey
findings.feasibilityAtN19: Narrows the feasible design space to inductive architectures before sample size is even considered; at n=19 the surviving inductive options would still be training a message-passing model on 19 independent units, which is not defensible.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: Transductive: NO, categorically. Inductive: possible in principle, unproven for nutrients at an unmonitored node.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED (tier 3). The honest, deployable conclusion of this angle -- topology as FEATURES, not as ARCHITECTURE -- is supported from an unexpected direction: even in the flagship river-network GNN, the topology encoding is reportedly a CHEAP CLOSED-FORM DISTANCE-DECAY WEIGHT, not learned structure. Edges exist wherever segment i is anywhere upstream of segment j, with adjacency A_ij = 1/(1+exp(dist(i,j))) on standardised along-river outlet-to-outlet distance -- a quantity computable from NHDPlus alone with no sensor readings. Moreover, the paper's time-delay ablation reportedly showed a MONOTONE INCREASE IN ERROR as the upstream-influence delay was lengthened from 1 to 5 days. That independently echoes this project's own failed experiment (travel-time-shifted lagged weather, loso_r2 0.116 -> 0.019) and reinforces the project's pattern that hydrologically-motivated TEMPORAL routing keeps failing while static geometry keeps winning.
findings.effectSize: UNVERIFIED: time-delay 1 -> 5 days reportedly produced 'a general increase of RMSE' for both temperature and streamflow (figure only; no tabulated values). Adjacency requires only NHDPlus-computable along-network distance.
findings.splitProtocol: temporal-holdout (ablation reported within the global temporal split)
findings.feasibilityAtN19: Fully feasible. The distance-decay quantity is a deterministic geometric computation, not a learned parameter, so it consumes no degrees of freedom. Concretely: for each basin, compute the along-network distance from each contributing flowline to the outlet from NHDPlus, and summarise it (mean, median, 90th percentile, and the exp-decay-weighted contributing area) as static basin-shape features -- three to five numbers, not 19-basin-limited estimation.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: YES. This is the key asymmetry of the whole angle: TOPOLOGY-DERIVED FEATURES (upstream drainage area, Strahler order, along-network distance distribution, confluence position) are computable at an arbitrary ungauged pin from NHDPlus via the NLDI delineation the product already performs. UPSTREAM-SENSOR-READING features are not. Build only the former.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED (tier 3). SPARROW answers the mass-balance half of this question in exactly the shape this project needs, but with a decisive caveat. It calibrates a nonlinear regression on a few hundred monitored stations and then predicts nutrient flux/concentration/yield across a network two to four orders of magnitude larger (~62,000 ERF1 reaches at 1:500K; ~2.6M NHDPlus reaches at 1:100K), using an explicit INCREMENTAL-AREA MASS BALANCE with hand-specified attenuation/decay terms -- topology as model STRUCTURE, not as message passing -- and it requires NO observation at the prediction reach. THE CAVEAT: SPARROW distinguishes CONDITIONED predictions (which substitute the OBSERVED station load on reaches that have a monitoring station, so downstream reaches inherit an observation-corrected upstream flux) from UNCONDITIONED ones. An arbitrary Iowa pin with no upstream gauge can only ever receive an UNCONDITIONED prediction. Any published SPARROW accuracy figure that is conditioned on observed upstream loads must be DISCARDED as evidence for this product.
findings.effectSize: Categorical by construction: conditioned > unconditioned accuracy, and only conditioned requires upstream observations. USGS/RSPARROW guidance reportedly notes unconditioned predictions 'are most representative of the model skill and performance at monitored and unmonitored stream locations.'
findings.splitProtocol: unknown -- agency documentation does not state a holdout design for the accuracy characterisations quoted
findings.nBasins: hundreds of calibration stations predicting onto ~62,000 to ~2.6M reaches
findings.feasibilityAtN19: Do NOT attempt to CALIBRATE a SPARROW-style model at n=19 (see the station-count finding below). DO consume SPARROW's already-published per-reach outputs as a static feature. Consuming a fitted national model costs zero degrees of freedom locally; fitting one costs many.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: YES in unconditioned mode -- that is SPARROW's entire purpose. Its published reach-level yields are joinable at any NHDPlus COMID including an arbitrary pin's outlet. NO in conditioned mode, which is unavailable without an upstream station.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED (tier 3). Two structural limits bound how much SPARROW-style mass balance can buy here. (a) TEMPORAL: SPARROW is reportedly a steady-state LONG-TERM MEAN ANNUAL model -- predictions 'reflect long-term mean annual nutrient conditions', standardised to a base year and de-trended to mean flow. It has NO daily dynamics, so it speaks ONLY to the between-site absolute-level term. That is actually well matched to this project (between_r2 0.21 is the weak term, daily timing is already good), but it means SPARROW can only ever contribute a static level prior, never a timing signal. (b) ACCURACY AT UNGAUGED REACHES IS COARSE: for the 2012 Mississippi/Atchafalaya River Basin models, the prediction accuracy of mean annual flux in UNMONITORED reaches is reportedly 'within 55-76% of the mean (RMSE)'. That is a 55-76% relative error on a long-term ANNUAL average -- a weak bar, and a realistic ceiling estimate for what pure topology-plus-mass-balance buys at an ungauged location.
findings.effectSize: UNVERIFIED: unmonitored-reach RMSE reportedly 55-76% of the mean for mean annual flux, described as ~20% lower error than prior SPARROW generations.
findings.splitProtocol: unknown -- the source article was inaccessible (HTTP 403); figures come from search/agency summaries
findings.feasibilityAtN19: Consuming the output is feasible; the finding sets expectations rather than blocking anything. It says: a SPARROW yield feature is a coarse level prior, likely worth a modest between-site gain, not a solution to the between-site gap.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: Yes -- these are explicitly unmonitored-reach numbers. But note the target quantity (mean annual flux) is not the product's target (daily max concentration >= 10 mg/L), so the figure is not a performance forecast for this project, only a bound on the informativeness of the prior.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED (tier 3). Published SPARROW calibrations reportedly use station counts 10x to 40x larger than this project's 19 independent basin families: a multi-agency regional nutrient effort compiled 2,739 monitoring sites from 73 agencies across major river basins MRB1-MRB7, with per-model counts ranging from 178 sites (MRB7 total nitrogen) to 810 sites (MRB3 total phosphorus), against a network of roughly 240,588 reaches. n=19 sits an ORDER OF MAGNITUDE BELOW the SMALLEST published SPARROW calibration. Therefore: fitting our own SPARROW-style routed regression with more than a handful of free source/decay coefficients would be overparameterised. No minimum-station or degrees-of-freedom threshold is stated in the source; the emphasis is reportedly on representativeness of the calibration set rather than raw count, which is itself a caution given Iowa-only sites are a narrow slice of catchment space.
findings.effectSize: UNVERIFIED: 2,739 sites total; 178 (MRB7 TN) to 810 (MRB3 TP) per model; reported calibration site density 0.15 to 1.09 sites per 1,000 km2.
findings.splitProtocol: unknown
findings.feasibilityAtN19: INFEASIBLE as a fitting exercise. This is the clearest n=19 disqualification in the angle: do not fit a bespoke mass-balance/routed regression. Feasible degenerate version: a ONE-PARAMETER or ZERO-PARAMETER area-weighted mixing feature (see datasets/howToIncorporate) that is computed, not estimated.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: The fitted-model route is blocked by sample size, not by the pin. The consume-published-outputs route works at any pin.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED (tier 3), and flagged as a likely OVERREACH TRAP. USGS reportedly states SPARROW models 'explain about 90% of the spatial variability in the log-transformed values of mean annual flux', and a resolution comparison reports yield R2 of 0.908 (NHD-resolution) vs 0.759 (coarser RF1) for total nitrogen and 0.810 vs 0.712 for total phosphorus. The tempting read -- 'mass-balance topology explains 90% of between-site variance, so it will fix our between_r2 0.21' -- is WRONG and must not be made: log mean-annual FLUX is dominated by drainage area and discharge, both trivially predictable, and these are in-sample CALIBRATION fits at MONITORED stations on long-term annual aggregates, not spatial holdouts on daily values. The one genuinely useful signal here is the resolution comparison: finer network resolution reportedly improved the AREA-NORMALISED (yield) term materially, which is weak support for computing our topology features from NHDPlus at 1:100K rather than a coarser network.
findings.effectSize: UNVERIFIED: ~0.90 R2 on log mean annual flux; yield R2 TN 0.908 (NHD) vs 0.759 (RF1), TP 0.810 vs 0.712. NOT comparable to LOFO daily numbers under rule 1.
findings.splitProtocol: unknown, probably in-sample calibration fit -- the source table was not directly retrievable (403)
findings.feasibilityAtN19: N/A as a method. Listed primarily as a warning: this is the number in the corpus most likely to be misquoted as justification for the angle.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: The quoted fits are at monitored stations, so no. The resolution lesson (use the finer network) applies at any pin.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED (tier 3). Uncertainty estimates reportedly COLLAPSE at unmonitored sites in the 70-segment Delaware forecasting study: 90% confidence intervals contained the observation only ~60% of the time at ungauged locations versus ~90% at gauged ones. Models trained on monitored sites are systematically OVERCONFIDENT when applied to unmonitored ones. Directly relevant to this product's operating point (beta=2, recall 0.864, 59% of alarms false): the calibrated probabilities produced under LOFO should be assumed MISCALIBRATED at a genuinely novel pin unless separately validated, and the deployed false-alarm rate at real pins should be expected to be worse than the LOFO estimate, not equal to it.
findings.effectSize: UNVERIFIED: 90% CI empirical coverage ~60% ungauged vs ~90% gauged.
findings.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout (5-fold spatial CV)
findings.feasibilityAtN19: Actionable and cheap regardless of sample size: report calibration (reliability curve, Brier decomposition) computed ONLY on LOFO-held-out families, never pooled with in-fold predictions, and treat the deployed threshold as needing a safety margin.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: This is a warning ABOUT the ungauged pin, and one of the few findings here that should change product behaviour rather than model architecture.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED (tier 3). Where network topology is COMPLICATED by structures that break advective connectivity, the graph prior reportedly turns NEGATIVE: in the 70-segment Delaware study, forecasts were worse for locations directly downstream from reservoirs. The adjacency encodes advective connectivity, and a physical structure that violates that assumption makes the prior harmful. IOWA ANALOGUE, stated as a hypothesis not a result: subsurface TILE DRAINAGE -- already flagged in this project as the dominant unmodelled Iowa hydrologic control -- routes water in ways a surface NHDPlus flow topology does not represent, as do impoundments and drainage ditches. That is a reason to expect a pure NHDPlus-adjacency graph to be MORE misleading in Iowa than in the Delaware basin, not less.
findings.effectSize: Qualitative -- direction stated (worse), magnitude not quantified in the accessible text.
findings.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout (2 of the 6 held-out test segments per fold were reservoir-impacted)
findings.feasibilityAtN19: The Iowa extension is an inference by the extractor, not a published finding, and is unverified twice over. It should be treated as a risk to note, not a result to cite.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: Argues against graph adjacency at Iowa pins specifically.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED (tier 3). A second Delaware graph-architecture comparison (RGCN vs Graph WaveNet, daily stream temperature) reportedly found the two architectures statistically INDISTINGUISHABLE when test data were well represented in training (1.64 vs 1.65 degC RMSE), with Graph WaveNet ahead in 4 of 5 experiments whose test partitions represented unseen environmental conditions. CRITICAL LIMITATION: no held-out-UNMONITORED-REACH RMSE is reported in any accessible text; the headline figures are monitored reaches under a temporal split, and the paper's contribution is explainability of WHY one graph architecture generalises better, not a demonstration that graph structure enables unmonitored-node prediction. Full text was paywalled (HTTP 403), so this rests on abstract-level metadata only -- the thinnest evidence in this angle.
findings.effectSize: UNVERIFIED: 1.64 vs 1.65 degC (a 0.6% difference, i.e. NO architectural advantage in-distribution); Graph WaveNet better in 4/5 out-of-distribution experiments, magnitudes unavailable.
findings.splitProtocol: unknown -- headline numbers appear to be a temporal split at monitored reaches; the 'geographic hold-out scenarios' referenced in the abstract could not be characterised
findings.nBasins: unknown -- Delaware River Basin reach network; associated USGS DRB data releases describe 456 river reaches, while the related RGCN work used a 42-segment subset. The paper's own reach count could not be confirmed.
findings.feasibilityAtN19: Weakly relevant. Its useful content is negative: architecture choice among graph models is near-zero in-distribution, which again points effort away from architecture.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: Cannot be determined from accessible material -- report as undetermined, not as supportive.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED (tier 3), and reported here as an EVIDENCE-ACCESS FAILURE rather than a result. The primary SPARROW documentation (Schwarz, Hoos, Alexander & Smith 2006, USGS Techniques and Methods 6-B3, 248 pp.) returned HTTP 403 on every attempted fetch -- the PDF, the landing page, and a full-text institutional mirror -- so only the bibliographic record was retrievable. Every SPARROW claim in this angle is therefore SECOND-HAND, sourced from USGS web pages and peer-reviewed applications rather than from the method's own specification. Combined with the total absence of adversarial verification, SPARROW claims in this angle should be treated as the weakest-supported material here and re-checked against tm6b3 before any of them is used to justify work.
findings.effectSize: Source unreachable; HTTP 403 Forbidden.
findings.splitProtocol: not-applicable
findings.feasibilityAtN19: N/A. Remedy is cheap: request the PDF via a USGS publications warehouse mirror or interlibrary route before relying on any SPARROW formulation detail.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: N/A.

datasets.name: NHDPlus Version 2 -- PlusFlowlineVAA (Value Added Attributes) and PlusFlow routing tables
datasets.resolution: 1:100,000 stream reach (COMID); ~2.6M reaches nationally; catchment polygons per COMID (~1 km2 median)
datasets.years: Static snapshot (NHDPlus V2, 2012 base network; NHDPlus HR available separately at 1:24,000 where published)
datasets.access: Bulk download by Vector Processing Unit (7z archives) from the EPA page; programmatic access via the Python pynhd / hyriver stack (pynhd.NHDPlusVAA) or the USGS ScienceBase-hosted national VAA table; NLDI web service for on-the-fly upstream navigation (https://labs.waterdata.usgs.gov/api/nldi/). No authentication.
datasets.coversMultiState: YES -- national, so basins extending into Minnesota, South Dakota, Nebraska, Missouri and Illinois are fully covered. This is a direct fix for the project's known inner-join under-count on large multi-state basins, for the topology terms at least.
datasets.whyUseful: This is the deployable core of the whole angle. It supplies the topology-derived STATIC features that are the only part of the river-network literature that survives contact with the deployment target: they are computable at an arbitrary ungauged map pin, they require no upstream sensor, they cost no degrees of freedom to estimate, and they are pure BETWEEN-SITE information -- the term where essentially all of this project's remaining headroom sits (between_r2 0.21 vs within_r2 0.42). The product already delineates the pin's basin via NLDI, so the marginal work is a table join on COMIDs it already has.
datasets.howToIncorporate: The project already stores an NHDPlus comid per basin and already runs NLDI navigation. Step 1, outlet features: join the outlet COMID to PlusFlowlineVAA and create, per site, `strahler_order_outlet` (StreamOrde), `total_drainage_area_km2` (TotDASqKM -- note this is the NHDPlus-accumulated area, immune to the Iowa-clipped inner-join undercount, so also create `area_ratio = TotDASqKM / existing log_basin_area` as a DIAGNOSTIC of how much basin area the current pipeline is losing outside Iowa), `arbolate_sum_km` (ArbolateSu, total upstream channel length -- a drainage-density proxy), `reach_slope` (SLOPE), and `pathlength_to_terminus_km` (Pathlength). Step 2, network-shape features aggregated over the delineated basin's flowline set (NLDI navigate upstreamTributaries from the pin): `max_strahler_in_basin`, `mean_strahler_area_weighted` (mean StreamOrde weighted by each flowline's catchment area), `n_confluences` (count of COMIDs with in-degree >= 2 in PlusFlow restricted to the basin), `confluence_density = n_confluences / TotDASqKM`, `drainage_density_km_per_km2 = sum(LENGTHKM) / TotDASqKM`, and `mainstem_length_fraction = length of the longest upstream path / arbolate sum` (a shape/elongation measure separating long thin basins from compact ones). Step 3, the distance-decay term borrowed from the Delaware adjacency formulation: for each contributing flowline compute along-network distance d to the outlet, then create `decay_weighted_area = sum_i(area_i / (1 + exp(z(d_i))))` on standardised distance, plus `dist_to_outlet_p50` and `dist_to_outlet_p90`. These generalise the existing mean_dist_to_sensor / max_dist_to_sensor static features from Euclidean to ALONG-NETWORK distance, which is the cheap version of what the GNN adjacency encodes. Step 4, position: `dist_to_next_downstream_confluence_km` and `upstream_area_fraction_above_nearest_confluence`. All of these are ~15 static scalars per site -- add them to the existing 5 static features and re-run LOFO, watching between_rate_r2 specifically rather than pooled AUC, since pooled metrics are dominated by the already-good within-site term.
datasets.limitations: (1) Static -- no temporal signal at all, consistent with the project's finding that temporal features keep failing and geometry keeps winning, but it means this cannot help the timing term. (2) NHDPlus V2 surface topology does NOT represent subsurface TILE DRAINAGE, which is the dominant Iowa hydrologic control; a tiled headwater's effective drainage network is not its mapped one, so these features are a systematically biased proxy in the most intensively tiled parts of the state. (3) At n=19 independent families, adding ~15 correlated static features risks overfitting the between-site term: introduce them in small correlated groups (area/order first, then shape, then distance-decay) and evaluate each group under LOFO, do not dump all 15 in at once. (4) TotDASqKM and StreamOrde are strongly collinear with the existing log_basin_area feature -- expect much of the gain to be already captured, and check permutation importance against the incumbent rather than in isolation.

datasets.name: EPA StreamCat -- NHDPlus catchment and watershed-accumulated landscape metrics
datasets.resolution: Per NHDPlus V2 COMID, in two flavours: 'Cat' (local catchment only) and 'Ws' (full upstream watershed, ALREADY ROUTED AND ACCUMULATED through the river network), ~2.6M reaches
datasets.years: Varies by metric; NLCD-derived layers at 2001/2006/2011/2016/2019, agricultural-nitrogen and fertilizer layers at their source vintages, soils/geology/climate static
datasets.access: Bulk CSV/zip per state or per VPU from the EPA FTP/HTTPS directory; StreamCat REST API at https://api.epa.gov/StreamCat/streams/metrics ; also via the R StreamCatTools package. No authentication, no cost.
datasets.coversMultiState: YES -- national coverage, and crucially the 'Ws' accumulation is performed on the NATIONAL network, so a basin extending into Minnesota or Missouri is accumulated correctly with no work by us.
datasets.whyUseful: This is the highest-value practical item in the angle, and it is 'mass-balance topology' delivered as pre-computed columns rather than as a model to fit. The project's known data problems include a silent inner-join undercount of crop area and nitrogen surplus for basins extending outside Iowa (worst for the largest, most influential multi-state basins) and 16.5% of grid cells lacking crop/surplus data. StreamCat's 'Ws' metrics are area-weighted upstream accumulations computed nationally, which structurally eliminates that undercount for every attribute it carries. It also supplies static catchment attributes of exactly the kind the CONUS prediction-in-unmonitored-basins finding reports as the single largest error reduction, and it carries candidate proxies for the missing tile-drainage control (hydrologic soil group, soil permeability, clay content, base-flow index, wetland/depression storage).
datasets.howToIncorporate: For each site (and for an arbitrary pin at inference), take the outlet COMID and pull the 'Ws' variants of: percent cropland and pasture (NLCD PctCrop2019Ws, PctHay2019Ws), agricultural nitrogen inputs (fertilizer and manure N metrics, e.g. FertWs / ManureWs where available), synthetic-nitrogen and biological-N-fixation layers, soil properties (ClayWs, SandWs, PermWs, OmWs), hydrology (BFIWs base-flow index, RunoffWs), impoundment/dam density (DamDensWs, DamNIDStorWs), road-stream crossings, and elevation/slope. Create features named `sc_ws_<metric>` and use them to REPLACE the current same-bucket CDL and nitrogen-surplus aggregates for the whole-basin term while KEEPING the existing distance-bucketed CDL features for the near-field signal -- i.e. run the ablation `distance-bucketed CDL only` vs `+ sc_ws_* whole-basin accumulations`, since the two encode different things (spatial arrangement vs correctly-accumulated total). Additionally compute `sc_undercount_ratio = sc_ws_PctCrop * TotDASqKM / (current pipeline's crop area)` as a per-site diagnostic to quantify exactly how much the inner-join is losing on multi-state basins -- that number is worth knowing on its own. For the BFI metric in particular, `sc_ws_BFI` is the best available free proxy for the baseflow-dominated, tile-influenced hydrology that the project flags as its dominant missing control, and it is computable at any pin.
datasets.limitations: (1) StreamCat's agricultural-nitrogen layers are themselves vintage-limited and may share upstream data lineage with the gTREND N-surplus product that already ends in 2017 -- check provenance before treating them as an independent fix for the post-2017 NaN problem. (2) Static-in-time or coarse-in-time; will not help the daily term. (3) High dimensionality (hundreds of metrics) against n=19 independent families: pre-select a small, hypothesis-driven set (N inputs, BFI, clay/permeability, dam storage, percent crop) rather than screening the full catalogue, which at 19 units would find spurious winners with near-certainty. (4) NLCD-derived crop percentages are less crop-class-specific than CDL, so this complements rather than replaces the existing CDL features.

datasets.name: USGS Select Attributes for NHDPlus V2.1 Reach Catchments and Modified Network Routed Upstream Watersheds (Wieczorek, Jackson & Schwarz)
datasets.resolution: Per NHDPlus V2.1 COMID; both local-catchment (CAT), total-upstream-accumulated (TOT), and divergence-routed (ACC) versions
datasets.years: Attribute-dependent (NLCD 2001-2019, STATSGO soils, PRISM climate normals, population, groundwater, dams)
datasets.access: ScienceBase bulk download (zipped TXT/CSV per attribute theme); no authentication; also mirrored through the nhdplusTools / pynhd attribute retrieval helpers
datasets.coversMultiState: YES -- national, accumulation performed on the national network including divergence routing
datasets.whyUseful: A second, USGS-maintained source of ALREADY-ROUTED upstream accumulations, overlapping StreamCat but with different themes (notably groundwater/well data, population, dams, and a divergence-aware accumulation that StreamCat does not provide). Useful both as an independent cross-check on StreamCat's accumulations -- a cheap way to detect whether an accumulation artefact is driving any observed gain -- and as the source for themes StreamCat lacks. This is the closest free national analogue to the GAGES-II static-attribute set that the CONUS unmonitored-basins work reportedly found most valuable, but unlike GAGES-II it is defined at EVERY reach rather than only at gauged basins, which is what an arbitrary pin needs.
datasets.howToIncorporate: Join the outlet COMID to the TOT (total upstream accumulated) tables and create `usgs_tot_<theme>` features for: STATSGO hydrologic soil group fractions and available water capacity, PRISM 30-year mean annual precipitation and temperature (as a CLIMATOLOGICAL between-site normal, distinct from the same-day weather scalars already in the model -- this is a static level term, not a temporal one, and the project's pattern is that static geography wins), dam storage and count, and population/housing density. Then run the same LOFO ablation protocol as for StreamCat. Where a theme exists in both sources, compute both and check they agree to within a few percent before trusting either.
datasets.limitations: (1) Substantial redundancy with StreamCat -- do not add both versions of the same attribute; pick one per theme. (2) Same n=19 overfitting caution: this catalogue is large enough to guarantee spurious selection if screened exhaustively. (3) Attribute vintages vary and are not aligned to the 2008-2026 study window; all are effectively static covariates.

datasets.name: USGS SPARROW model outputs -- regional nutrient models (MRB1-MRB7) and the 2012 Mississippi/Atchafalaya (MARB) models, per-reach predicted nitrogen load, yield and incremental yield
datasets.resolution: Per stream reach on the NHDPlus (1:100K) or ERF1 (1:500K) network, depending on model vintage; ~62,000 to ~2.6M reaches
datasets.years: Steady-state long-term mean annual conditions standardised to a base year (2002 and 2012 vintages are the common ones); no time series
datasets.access: SPARROW Decision Support System / mapper (https://sparrow.wim.usgs.gov/) for interactive extraction; per-model data releases on ScienceBase with reach-level prediction tables as CSV; RSPARROW (R package) for running published model specifications. Free, no authentication.
datasets.coversMultiState: YES -- the MARB/MRB models cover the entire Mississippi basin, so Iowa basins extending into neighbouring states are covered natively.
datasets.whyUseful: This is the mass-balance half of the research question delivered as a joinable NUMBER instead of a model to fit -- which matters enormously given that the smallest published SPARROW calibration reportedly used 178 stations against our 19 independent families. A SPARROW predicted mean-annual total-nitrogen YIELD at the pin's outlet reach is a single static scalar encoding routed upstream sources minus attenuation: precisely a BETWEEN-SITE ABSOLUTE LEVEL prior, which is the term this project is weakest on. It requires no observation at the prediction reach (unconditioned mode) and is therefore available at an arbitrary map pin.
datasets.howToIncorporate: Join the basin outlet COMID to the SPARROW reach prediction table and create three features: `sparrow_tn_yield_kg_km2_yr` (total nitrogen yield, area-normalised -- the between-site level prior), `sparrow_tn_incremental_yield` (the local incremental-area contribution, which separates 'this basin generates a lot' from 'this basin inherits a lot from upstream'), and `sparrow_tn_delivery_fraction` (the modelled fraction of local load surviving to the outlet, i.e. the attenuation term). Then test as a small block under LOFO, reporting between_rate_r2 as the primary metric. CRITICAL: use the UNCONDITIONED predictions only. Conditioned predictions substitute observed station loads and are unavailable at an ungauged pin -- and worse, using conditioned values at our 85 training sites while an arbitrary pin gets unconditioned values would create a train/serve skew that LOFO would not detect. Verify which mode the downloaded table contains before use.
datasets.limitations: (1) LEAKAGE RISK, must be checked first: SPARROW's Mississippi-basin calibration stations plausibly include Iowa nitrate monitoring sites that are also in our training set. If a training site's own observed load informed the SPARROW coefficients, the feature is partially contaminated and LOFO will overstate its value -- cross-check the SPARROW calibration station list against the 85 sites and, at minimum, report the overlap. (2) Steady-state mean annual only: no daily dynamics, contributes only to the between-site level term. (3) Vintage ends at the model base year (2012 for MARB), so like the gTREND N-surplus it does not track post-base-year change -- but unlike gTREND it would be used as a STATIC site attribute rather than broadcast forward as a time-varying value, which avoids the project's known -0.166 failure mode from broadcasting 2017 N-surplus forward. (4) All SPARROW claims in this angle are unverified and second-hand; the primary specification (USGS TM 6-B3) was inaccessible (HTTP 403). (5) Reported ungauged-reach accuracy (unverified) is 55-76% relative RMSE on mean annual flux -- a coarse prior, so expect a modest between-site gain at best.

datasets.name: USGS NLDI (Network-Linked Data Index) -- upstream/downstream navigation and linked feature discovery
datasets.years: Live service against the static NHDPlus V2 network
datasets.access: Public REST API (no key, no authentication); Python via pynhd, R via nhdplusTools. Endpoints: /linked-data/comid/position for pin-to-COMID snapping, /navigation/UT and /UM for upstream tributary and upstream mainstem traversal, /navigation/UT/nwissite to enumerate USGS sites upstream.
datasets.whyUseful: Already in the product's delineation path, but two capabilities are underused. First, it is the mechanism that makes every topology feature above computable at an arbitrary pin -- it is the reason 'topology as features' is deployable while 'topology as architecture' is not. Second, its /navigation/UT/nwissite endpoint answers, at inference time and for free, the single question that decides whether ANY upstream-observation method could ever apply at a given pin: is there a monitored site upstream, and how far? Given the corpus's repeated finding that graph methods fail precisely at headwater nodes with no monitored upstream neighbour, knowing this per-pin is directly operational.
datasets.howToIncorporate: Two uses. (a) FEATURE: at both training and inference, call /navigation/UT/nwissite (and the equivalent against the project's own 85-site registry, since 61 IWQIS sites are not USGS sites) and create `n_monitored_upstream`, `dist_to_nearest_upstream_monitor_km`, and `frac_basin_area_monitored_upstream`. These are computable at any pin. (b) PRODUCT GUARDRAIL, probably the higher-value use: use `n_monitored_upstream == 0` to identify pins in the regime where the literature says transfer is hardest, and either widen the predicted uncertainty band or surface a confidence caveat in the UI for those pins. This operationalises the unverified-but-consistent finding that ungauged-node performance and calibration both degrade sharply, and it costs one API call. Note the honest framing: this does NOT let us USE upstream readings at a novel pin (there usually are none, and relying on them would break the deployment target); it lets us KNOW when we are in the hard regime.
datasets.limitations: (1) Rate-limited public service; cache the traversal per pin rather than calling repeatedly. (2) Traversal on very large multi-state basins returns large flowline sets and can be slow -- pre-compute for the 85 training sites, and consider a distance cap at inference. (3) NHDPlus V2 resolution only; small tiled headwater channels are under-represented, which is the same tile-drainage blind spot noted above.

datasets.name: GAGES-II -- Geospatial Attributes of Gages for Evaluating Streamflow
datasets.resolution: Per gauged basin (9,322 basins), ~2,000 static attributes
datasets.years: Attributes referenced to varying vintages; basin set fixed
datasets.access: ScienceBase bulk download (shapefiles + attribute tables); no authentication
datasets.coversMultiState: National, but ONLY at gauged basins -- not at arbitrary locations.
datasets.whyUseful: Named here only because the CONUS prediction-in-unmonitored-basins finding (the highest-ranked finding in this angle) reportedly attributes its largest single error reduction to adding GAGES-II static catchment attributes. It is listed so the lead is not lost -- but with an explicit warning about its applicability.
datasets.howToIncorporate: Do NOT build the production feature set on GAGES-II: it is defined at 9,322 gauged basins, not at arbitrary pins, so a feature engineered from it cannot be computed at the deployment target. Correct use is twofold: (a) as a SPECIFICATION -- read which attribute families drove the reported gain (soils, geology, climate normals, land cover, hydrologic disturbance indices) and then source the equivalent quantities from StreamCat/Wieczorek 'Ws'/'TOT' accumulations, which ARE defined everywhere; (b) as a pooling aid if out-of-state training sites are ever added at USGS gauges, where GAGES-II attributes exist by construction.
datasets.limitations: Defined only at gauged basins -- the single disqualifying limitation for this product. Any evaluation using GAGES-II attributes at our 85 sites would be optimistic relative to what an arbitrary pin can receive, unless every attribute used has a verified everywhere-defined equivalent.

refuted.claim: 'River-network GNNs improve prediction at unmonitored nodes' -- as a general, transferable statement.
refuted.status: NOT SUPPORTED by anything in this corpus (all evidence unverified; no tier-1 claim exists to refute or confirm it).
refuted.detail: Across the sources reached: HydroNets was reportedly evaluated under a TEMPORAL holdout only with every node gauged and the target's own past readings as an input, so it contributes zero unmonitored-node evidence; the survey reportedly found only three GNN-at-unmonitored-sites studies, none for water quality, with no quantitative held-out-node metrics; the RGCN-vs-Graph-WaveNet comparison reports no held-out-unmonitored-reach RMSE in accessible text; and the 70-segment Delaware forecasting study reportedly found the plain LSTM generally best overall, with the graph models winning only on a conditional high-temperature subset. The only genuine held-out-node gain located is n=5 simulated-ungauged segments inside a 76%-monitored 42-segment graph, and even there the graph-only variant reportedly lost to a plain RNN at the headwater case. The correct statement of the state of evidence is: unproven for nutrients at genuinely unmonitored nodes, and contradicted at the specific node type (headwater, no monitored upstream neighbour) that dominates this product's use case.

refuted.claim: 'The RGCN-with-data-assimilation result shows graph models are best for ungauged locations.'
refuted.status: MISLEADING as stated (unverified corpus, but internally contradicted).
refuted.detail: Two extractions from the same paper conflict in emphasis: one presents RGCN-DA as best at ungauged locations, another reports that the plain LSTM was 'generally the best performing model when considering all temperature observations' and that RGCN/RGCN-DA won only on the >18 degC subset. Separately, the data-assimilation component reportedly requires observations at or near the target site to update model states via an ensemble Kalman filter -- the paper's own stated mechanism is that DA lets the network 'borrow information from nearby monitored sites'. That mechanism is unavailable at an arbitrary Iowa pin with no nitrate history and no guaranteed monitored upstream neighbour. So even taking the favourable reading at face value, the gain is conditional on a dense, hydrologically connected monitored neighbourhood, which the deployment target does not have. Unresolved because verification was cut.

refuted.claim: 'A graph over our 85 sites built from site similarity/proximity would add information.'
refuted.status: ARGUED AGAINST by an unverified survey-level design criticism.
refuted.detail: The survey reportedly states that graphs constructed from site characteristics or location alone 'introduce no new information (e.g., physical connectivity) beyond what' is already in those characteristics, and that graphs built from real physical connections have so far been seen only in stream-network modelling. Our XGBoost already ingests lat, lon, log_basin_area and distance features directly, so a similarity graph would be largely redundant with the existing feature set. Only a genuine upstream-downstream connectivity graph could add structure -- and ours covers 28 upstream_uid / 40 downstream_uid links across 85 sites, a sparse and mostly disconnected graph.

refuted.claim: 'Network-structure methods require hundreds of catchments (CAMELS-scale), so they are infeasible at n=19.'
refuted.status: PARTIALLY REFUTED on node count, but the constraint reappears in a different form.
refuted.detail: Two unverified data points push back on the node-count version of the objection: the Delaware graph work used 42 river segments and HydroNets used 39- and 13-node trees, all comparable to or smaller than our 85 sites. So raw node count is NOT the barrier. The barrier is MONITORED FRACTION and independent spatial units: those graphs were 43-100% gauged, whereas the Iowa deployment scenario places the prediction node in an essentially unmonitored neighbourhood, and our 85 sites collapse to 19 independent families under leak-safe CV. State the objection correctly: not 'too few nodes' but 'too few independently informative, monitored, connected nodes near the prediction point'.

refuted.claim: 'SPARROW explains ~90% of spatial variability, so mass-balance topology can largely close our between-site gap.'
refuted.status: REJECTED as an inference, even taking the underlying unverified figure at face value.
refuted.detail: The ~0.90 figure is reportedly R2 on LOG MEAN ANNUAL FLUX at MONITORED calibration stations -- a quantity dominated by drainage area and discharge scaling, which is trivially predictable, aggregated over years rather than daily, and fitted in-sample rather than under spatial holdout. Under research rule 1 it is not comparable to this project's LOFO daily numbers and must not be quoted alongside them. The comparable figure for the actual deployment situation is the unconditioned-prediction accuracy at UNMONITORED reaches, reportedly 55-76% relative RMSE on mean annual flux -- a far weaker bar and the realistic ceiling for what topology-plus-mass-balance buys at an ungauged pin.

refuted.claim: 'Multi-day advective routing of upstream information will help, if implemented properly through the network.'
refuted.status: ARGUED AGAINST by an unverified ablation that independently echoes this project's own failure.
refuted.detail: The Delaware paper's time-delay ablation reportedly produced 'a general increase of RMSE' as the upstream-influence delay was lengthened from 1 to 5 days, for both temperature and streamflow. This project already implemented advective travel-time routing (weather per distance bucket shifted by median flow distance / 2.1 m/s) and it was part of the lagged-weather failure (loso_r2 0.116 -> 0.019). Two independent negative signals on the same idea. Do not re-propose deeper or better-tuned temporal routing without a new mechanism; the consistent pattern in both this project and this corpus is that static geometry wins and temporal routing does not.

uncovered: EVERYTHING IN THIS ANGLE IS UNCOVERED IN THE STRICT SENSE: tier1_survived and tier1_refuted are both EMPTY. The original search agent for this angle died and it was re-researched after adversarial verification had been cut for budget. No claim, number, protocol description, or dataset detail above has been checked against its primary source. The corpus's documented failure mode is confident overreach from thin evidence -- correct conclusion, wrong warrant or misattributed effect size -- so directional reads are usable as leads and numeric reads are not usable as evidence.

GNN or graph-based prediction for a NUTRIENT or NITRATE target at a held-out unmonitored node: NOTHING FOUND, and one survey reportedly states affirmatively that no such study exists in its scope. Every river-network graph result located is stream TEMPERATURE or STREAMFLOW. Whether nitrate's very different generation process (tile-drain-dominated, agronomically driven, strongly seasonal, threshold-exceedance framed) behaves like temperature under spatial transfer is entirely unstudied here.

Any BINARY EXCEEDANCE / CLASSIFICATION result from the river-network literature. Every located metric is a regression metric (RMSE, R2, NSE, R2-persist). There is no evidence about whether topology features help a classification target such as violation >= 10 mg/L, whether they shift PR-AUC or only AUC, or how they behave at an operating point like beta=2. This project's PRIMARY target is the classification one, so this gap is directly on the critical path.

The INCREMENTAL-AREA MASS BALANCE and USGS LOAD-ESTIMATION half of the research question is only thinly covered and entirely second-hand. The ML survey reportedly contained NO SPARROW, mass-balance, incremental-area, or load-estimation content at all -- mass conservation appeared only abstractly as a candidate knowledge-guided LOSS term, with cited successes in lake temperature, lake phosphorus and subsurface transport, none at unmonitored RIVER nodes. And the primary SPARROW specification (USGS TM 6-B3) returned HTTP 403 on every fetch. Specifically NOT covered: LOADEST and the WRTDS (Weighted Regressions on Time, Discharge, and Season) family, which are the standard USGS load-estimation tools and were never reached; whether any of them has an ungauged-site variant; and whether a WRTDS-style concentration-discharge relationship regionalised across our 19 families is viable.

NO QUANTIFIED MINIMUM MONITORED-NODE DENSITY for graph methods. This was an explicit part of the research question ('what network size and monitored-node density do published successes require?'). What was obtained is a set of point observations -- 76% of segments temperature-monitored and 43% flow-monitored in a 42-node Delaware graph, 100% gauged in 39- and 13-node HydroNets trees, SPARROW calibration densities of 0.15-1.09 stations per 1,000 km2 -- but NO study was found that varies monitored density and reports the breakdown point. The practical answer 'somewhere well above what an arbitrary Iowa pin has' is an inference from those point observations, not a measured threshold.

NO ABLATION ANYWHERE ISOLATING TOPOLOGY-AS-FEATURES from topology-as-architecture. The central recommendation of this angle -- add Strahler order, drainage area, network position and along-network distance as static features to a tabular model -- is an inference from the pattern of failures in the architecture literature plus this project's own history (geometry wins, temporal routing fails). No paper was found that adds NHDPlus topology attributes to a gradient-boosted or tabular model and reports the delta under a SPATIAL holdout. The expected effect size for the recommended action is therefore UNKNOWN, and the recommendation rests on cheapness and deployability rather than on demonstrated gain.

NO EVIDENCE ON TILE DRAINAGE and network topology interaction, despite tile drainage being flagged as the dominant Iowa hydrologic control. The corpus contains one qualitative signal that structures breaking advective connectivity (reservoirs) make the graph prior actively harmful, and the Iowa-tile-drainage extension of that is the extractor's inference, not a published result. No tile-drainage data source was identified in this angle either -- that remains an open acquisition problem, and it directly undermines the fidelity of any NHDPlus-surface-topology feature in the most intensively tiled catchments.

NO INFORMATION ON WHETHER THE 28 upstream_uid / 40 downstream_uid LINKS IN THIS PROJECT'S OWN DATA FORM A USABLE GRAPH. Nothing in the literature speaks to a 85-node graph with ~40 known edges and unknown edge completeness. Whether those links are a connected subnetwork or scattered pairs, and whether the linked pairs' records overlap in time, is a local data question that was not answerable from published sources and should be checked directly before any further consideration of graph methods.

THE LEAKAGE STATUS OF SPARROW OUTPUTS relative to this project's 85 sites is unresolved. If Iowa nitrate monitoring stations in our training set were also SPARROW calibration stations, a SPARROW-yield feature is partially contaminated and LOFO would overstate its value. The calibration station list was not obtained.

TOPP ET AL. (2023) full text was inaccessible (Wiley HTTP 403), so its reported 'geographic hold-out scenarios' could not be characterised -- neither the reach count, the monitored fraction, nor whether any held-out-unmonitored-reach error was reported. This is the one source in the angle most likely to contain a genuine spatial-holdout graph result, and it remains unread.

NO OUT-OF-STATE NITRATE NETWORK INVENTORY. The highest-ranked finding implies the remedy at n=19 is to POOL with more sites rather than add architecture, and the survey material reportedly warns specifically against building models on small homogeneous sets of watersheds for unmonitored prediction. But no concrete inventory of poolable out-of-state high-frequency nitrate networks (Illinois, Minnesota, Missouri, Nebraska, Upper Mississippi) -- with site counts, temporal coverage, sensor type, and access route -- was assembled. That is the single most valuable follow-up this angle points to, and it belongs to a different angle.
